headline: Russia and Ukraine Keep Hitting Energy Targets Despite Proposed Truce
seoTitle: Russia, Ukraine Continue Energy Strikes Despite Truce Proposal | FMB News
seoDescription: Russia struck petrol stations and energy infrastructure in Ukraine while Ukraine hit a Russian refinery, despite a U.S.-proposed halt to energy attacks.
deck: Russia struck petrol stations and other infrastructure in Ukraine while Kyiv said it hit a Russian oil refinery, even as a U.S.-proposed halt to energy attacks remained unresolved.
author: FMB News World Desk

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: Russia and Ukraine continued striking energy-related targets on September 15 despite a U.S. proposal for the two sides to stop attacks on each other’s energy infrastructure.

Reuters reported that Russia launched around 200 drones overnight, with Ukrainian officials saying attacks damaged petrol stations in Kyiv and energy and port infrastructure elsewhere and killed two people.

Ukraine, in turn, said it struck an oil refinery in Syzran in Russia’s Samara region as well as drone-production facilities in the Taganrog and Oryol regions. Russian regional officials confirmed strikes on industrial or warehouse facilities but did not independently confirm every Ukrainian description of the targets.

sections.heading: Context
paragraphs: U.S. President Donald Trump said on September 14 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed not to attack each other’s energy infrastructure, but Reuters reported that neither side had formally confirmed such an agreement at the time of the new strikes.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Kyiv was prepared to support an energy ceasefire if the United States could ensure that Moscow was genuinely prepared to follow through.
Repeated attacks on refineries, fuel depots, power systems and logistics have made energy infrastructure a major pressure point in the war and have contributed to tighter fuel markets.

sections.heading: Why this matters
paragraphs: Damage to refining and fuel infrastructure can affect supplies beyond the battlefield. Russia is a major energy producer, and refinery outages or export restrictions can tighten international diesel and petroleum-product markets.
For the Philippines, which imports most of its petroleum requirements, sustained global fuel-market pressure can feed into transport, electricity and logistics costs.

sections.heading: What to watch next
paragraphs: Watch whether a formal, verifiable energy-target ceasefire is established and whether both sides actually reduce strikes on refineries, fuel storage and power infrastructure.
Also watch Russian refinery output, fuel-export restrictions and global diesel prices, which can transmit the economic effects of the conflict far beyond Europe.

verificationNotes: Reuters reported the Russian strikes and Ukraine's claimed strike on the Syzran refinery; target descriptions from the belligerents are attributed rather than presented as independently verified in every detail.
The article distinguishes Trump's announcement of an energy truce from the lack of formal confirmation by both sides at the time of the strikes.
The photograph is a licensed contextual file image of Kyiv and does not depict the reported September 15 attacks.
